prayer.text: O Sacrament most holy, O Sacrament divine, all praise and all thanksgiving be every moment thine.

cues.text: In June 1453, the upper Susa Valley near Exilles, in the Alps northwest of Turin, had become a battlefield between the forces of Rene of Anjou and Duke Ludovico of Savoy.
Soldiers plundering the town broke into its church and stole among other valuables.
One man forced open the tabernacle and made off with a monstrance still holding a consecrated Host.
He wrapped it in a sack and loaded it onto a mule bound for Turin.
A Mule That Would Not Carry It

Reaching Turin's herb market, in front of the church of San Silvestro, the mule suddenly stumbled and collapsed to the ground, spilling the contents of the sack across the pavement in full view of the market crowd.
As witnesses looked on, the consecrated Host freed itself from the fallen sack and rose into the air on its own, hovering luminous above the surrounding houses.
A priest among the crowd hurried to summon the Bishop of Turin, Ludovico of Romagnano, who knelt in the square before the suspended Host and then rose, holding a sacred chalice above his head.
The Host, still shining, descended slowly through the air until it came to rest gently within the chalice the bishop held.

Unusually for an account this old, the event was recorded almost immediately in civil records: the Capitulary Acts of the city of Turin from 1454, 1455, and 1456 all reference the miracle, alongside contemporary writings of the municipality.
An iron railing inside what became the Basilica of Corpus Domini marks the exact spot of the mule's fall, inscribed with an account of the event still read by visitors today.
Popes Pius II, Benedict XIV, Clement XIII, Gregory XVI, St. Pius X, and Pius XI all recognized the Turin account across the centuries.
They granted indulgences to its pilgrims, and in 1928 Pius XI raised its church to the rank of minor basilica.
In 1853, marking the fourth centenary, Blessed Pius IX celebrated the anniversary with St. John Bosco himself in attendance.
This continued a five-century thread of devotion in a city later known worldwide for another sacred relic entirely, the Holy Shroud.
